original_question: How should one build a microscopic theory of large-amplitude collective motion at finite temperature, and what microscopic mechanisms govern damping and dissipation of those motions as one moves from yrast states toward the compound-nucleus regime?
target_in_paper: “Another vast unexplored field is the microscopic study of LACM at finite temperature. Microscopic mechanism of damping and dissipation of various kinds of LACM is a long-term subject. It seems particularly interesting to explore both theoretically and experimentally how the character of LACM changes when going from the yrast to the compound-nucleus regions.”
correct_elements: The draft question correctly identifies the need to develop a microscopic theory of large-amplitude collective motion (LACM) at finite temperature and to elucidate the microscopic mechanisms governing damping and dissipation, specifically as one moves from yrast states toward the compound-nucleus regime.
missing_details: Definition of LACM as large-amplitude collective motion in nuclear many-body systems
Clarification that “finite temperature” refers to non-zero thermal excitation in nuclei (beyond the zero-temperature setting)
Explicit reference to both theoretical formulation and experimental exploration
Explanation of “yrast states” as the lowest-energy states at given angular momentum and “compound-nucleus region” as high-level-density, thermalized nuclear states
Specification that this open problem is distinct from small-amplitude approximations and lies outside the zero-temperature framework discussed earlier
refined_question: How can one formulate a fully self-consistent microscopic theory of large-amplitude collective motion (LACM) in nuclei at finite temperature, and what are the underlying microscopic mechanisms of damping and dissipation that govern the evolution of these collective motions as one proceeds from low-lying yrast excitations to the compound-nucleus regime?
justification: The refined question is drawn verbatim from the open-problem statement in section 7 of the paper, adding necessary definitions and clarifications to make it self-contained and faithful to the authors’ intent. It preserves the focus on finite-temperature LACM, damping and dissipation mechanisms, and the transition from yrast to compound-nucleus conditions.
